messages:
marta: quick RFC follow-up — proposing we split the runtime into three latency lanes (hot / warm / cold) and wire a policy-based router. goal: pay down cross-cutting hotpath debt and make SLAs explicit. thoughts?

sam: curious — how different from the affinity demux work? sounds like another axis.

marta: good call. affinity demux is about tenant routing. lanes are about runtime resource scheduling + model choices. they can coexist. lanes give us an escape hatch for degraded hardware or heavy quantized models.

kevin: main concern is compatibility with our existing KV cache and session mesh. If requests move between lanes we must preserve cache semantics or accept higher miss rates.

anjali: +1 on cache concern. Also need to think about function-calling and streaming — warm/cold may add latency that breaks some customers.

luca: we should define clear SLO tiers first. e.g. hot: p95 < 50ms, warm: p95 < 250ms, cold: p95 < 1s. Then map model variants and kernels to lanes.

marta: yeah — provisional mapping in thread: hot -> FP16/fast kernel / pinned LRU cache; warm -> int8 quantized / batched; cold -> CPU-backed fallback or async queue.

sam: what about rollout? my mental flow: create policy config, add router + canary flag, route a small % to new lanes, validate tail latency + correctness on prompt set. If good, increase.

kevin: also need migration playbook for pinned sessions. If session X lives in hot and we move it to warm, we have to either warm the KV cache or gracefully rehydrate. Suggest: allow session pinning opt-in and a graceful TTL extension on migration.

anjali: observability checklist: per-lane token cost, p50/p95/p99, cold start rate, model divergence metrics (eval prompts). Add a synthetic probe that exercise function-calling paths every 30s.

luca: ops/config sketch for policy (proto idea):
```
router_policy:
  matchers:
    - expr: request.latency_slo <= 0.05 -> lane: hot
    - expr: model.size <= 2B and request.burstable -> lane: warm
    - default: cold
  fallthrough: true  # allow fallback to warm/hot if cold is overloaded
```

marta: love the sketch. fallthrough is critical — we want graceful degradation, not hard errors. Also need the model registry to expose "lane_compatibility" flag for each model artifact.

sam: minor implementation note: router should be deterministic per-request id to avoid oscillation during retries. sticky-hash based on session id + request id prefix?

kevin: security: lanes must preserve tenant isolation. hot lane is shared GPU; warm could be multitenant quantized. ensure encryption-in-transit + audit logs remain.

anjali: what's the expected infra cost delta? hot lane increases reserved GPU cost but should reduce tail latency and improve revenue signals. warm/cold shift lowers per-token cost. we need a cost model before wider rollout.

marta: action items:
- sam: spike router prototype + deterministic hashing (2w)
- kevin: cache migration playbook + TTL strategy (1w)
- anjali: observability probes + eval prompt set for regression detection (1w)
- luca: SLO definitions + cost model starter (1w)

marta: also: we should document compatibility matrix (model -> lane) in the model profile registry before any routing changes. @deploy-bot can we gate a canary once each action item is done?

deploy-bot: noted. will create canary checklist and add required approvals when the repo PRs are linked.

sam: OK. I'll post the router spike PR link here when ready. please flag any blocking constraints (esp. session rehydration).

kevin: one more risk: long-tail fanout. if warm lane batches aggressively, we might cause head-of-line blocking for short requests. include micro-batching limits per-lane.

marta: good call. add per-lane batch caps and a per-tenant burst window.

anjali: when we test, include a mix of developer CI tests + small production canary (1% traffic) for 48h. automated rollback on correctness/regression.

luca: +1. also capture a post-mortem template for any lane-related incidents.

marta: thanks all — this is the follow-up I wanted. if no objections, I'll convert the discussion into a short RFC addendum and schedule a sync.
